scenes.heading: Behaviour and ecology
scenes.sub: Why do animals do what they do?
scenes.say: Why do bees dance? Why do magpies swoop? Behaviour affects survival and reproduction, so natural selection shapes it.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of 'why'
scenes.say: Every behaviour has two explanations. Proximate is the process: how it happens, through stimuli, hormones and nerves. Ultimate is the use: why it evolved. A bird sings in spring because longer days change its hormones, and because singing wins mates and territory.

scenes.heading: Learning
points: Imprinting: goslings follow the first mover
Classical: link a neutral cue to a real one
Operant: sick after a bright insect? Avoid it
scenes.say: Innate behaviour works the first time without experience. Learning changes behaviour through experience. Habituation is birds learning to ignore a scarecrow. Imprinting is goslings following the first moving thing they see. And operant conditioning is a predator avoiding a bright insect that made it sick.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A delivery rider turns down small jobs when big orders are frequent
scenes.science: Foragers skip low-value prey when high-value prey is common
scenes.breaks: A shorebird doesn't do sums: natural selection favours behaviour close to the best energy rate, balanced against the risk of being eaten.
scenes.say: Picture a delivery rider. If big orders pop up every few minutes, you'd turn down every small job, however many there are. Foragers do the same. Whether they eat low-value prey depends on how common the best prey is, not the poor prey.

scenes.heading: Optimal diet
scenes.question: Large crab: 600 J, 20 s. Small crab: 150 J, 10 s. Large crabs are found every 30 s. Eat small crabs?
scenes.say: Profitability is energy over handling time. A small crab gives fifteen joules per second. If large crabs take thirty seconds to find, eating only large crabs gives six hundred over fifty: twelve joules per second. Fifteen beats twelve, so the bird should eat both.
scenes.caption: Profitability is energy ÷ handling time. A small crab gives 15 J per second. If large crabs take 30 s to find, eating only large crabs gives 600 ÷ 50: 12 J per second. 15 beats 12, so the bird should eat both.

scenes.heading: Hamilton's rule
scenes.say: Why help relatives? Hamilton's rule: help when relatedness times benefit beats cost. A bird helping its parents raise three extra full siblings scores zero point five times three: one point five. That beats the one offspring it gives up, so helping wins.
scenes.caption: Why help relatives? Hamilton's rule: help when relatedness × benefit beats cost. A bird helping its parents raise 3 extra full siblings scores 0.5 × 3 = 1.5. That beats the 1 offspring it gives up, so helping wins.

scenes.heading: Signals and mating
points: Costly signals tend to be honest
Bee waggle dance: direction and distance
scenes.say: Costly signals, like bright plumage, tend to be honest, because only healthy animals can afford them. Sexual selection works through competition within one sex and through mate choice. And honeybees waggle dance to show the direction and distance of food.

points: Costly signals tend to be honest
scenes.say: Quick recap. Proximate is how, ultimate is why. Learning includes habituation, imprinting and conditioning. Profitability is energy over handling time. Help relatives when r B is greater than C. And selection never acts for the good of the species. Now try the practice questions!
